passage: Every evening for two months, Joseph practised his badminton serve against the wall of their Mumbai building. The watchman got used to the tok-tok sound. At the colony tournament he reached the final against Zubin, who was a year older. Joseph's serves were clean, but Zubin was quicker at the net and won by three points. Joseph's throat felt tight. He walked to the net and shook Zubin's hand. "Your smashes are brilliant." Zubin grinned. "Your serve was tough to return. Practise with me on Sundays?"

qa.q: Where did Joseph practise his badminton serve?
qa.a: He practised against the wall of their Mumbai building.

qa.q: What does Joseph's tight throat suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt disappointed and close to tears after losing.

qa.q: Which choice by Joseph showed good sportsmanship?
qa.a: He shook Zubin's hand and praised Zubin's smashes despite feeling upset.

qa.q: How does Zubin respond to Joseph's grace?
qa.a: Zubin praises Joseph's serve and invites him to practise together, showing respect.

grounding: It shows a child building skill through practice and losing gracefully.

passage:
"We lost four–one, Tenzin." Dolma dumped her boots at the door.
"I saw. Your team was tired."
"I missed an easy goal. Everyone saw."
"Did you shake hands after?"
"Yes. I said 'good game.' But I wanted to cry."
"That's still good sport. What will you do?"
Dolma sat on the step. "Practise shooting. Every day before school."
"I'll be in goal. Six-thirty?"
She groaned, then smiled. "Fine. Six-thirty."

qa.q: What was the score of the match?
qa.a: They lost four–one.

qa.q: What does Dolma saying "I wanted to cry" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals she felt very disappointed and embarrassed about missing the goal.

qa.q: What plan does Dolma make to improve?
qa.a: She plans to practise shooting every day before school, with Tenzin in goal.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel supporting Dolma?
qa.a: Tenzin seems caring and willing to help, offering to get up early to play goalkeeper. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child losing gracefully and committing to repeated practice.

passage: I'm Bidisha. When I was twelve, our kabaddi team reached the district final. For weeks I'd practised my raids every evening in the school ground until my knees were scraped. In the final, Kalyani's team was faster. I got tagged out twice and we lost. I wanted to kick the mat. Instead, I lined up with everyone and shook hands. When I reached Kalyani, I said, "You were too good today." She said, "Your raid in the first half scared me." I didn't expect that. It made me want to practise even more for next year.

qa.q: What had Bidisha practised every evening?
qa.a: Bidisha practised raids in the school ground.

qa.q: What does Bidisha wanting to kick the mat show?
qa.a: It shows Bidisha felt angry and frustrated after losing.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha lose gracefully?
qa.a: Bidisha lined up, shook hands and congratulated Kalyani despite feeling frustrated.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Bidisha's congratulations?
qa.a: She seems to respect Bidisha, answering with praise for Bidisha's raid.

grounding: A first-person account of practising a sport and losing gracefully.

passage: Coach's note, junior badminton, Saturday. Pallavi (10) reached the final of the club tournament today. For six weeks she has come early to practise her low serve against the wall, even on days her friends skipped. Today it showed: her serves were clean. She lost the final in three games to a taller girl from Andheri. At the last point she threw her head back and I saw her blinking hard. But she walked straight to the net, shook hands and said, 'Good game, your smashes were amazing.' Only after that did she sit on the bench and cry into her towel. I sat beside her and said nothing for a while. On Monday we'll look at her backhand. — Coach Himani

qa.q: What did Pallavi practise early for six weeks?
qa.a: She practised her low serve against the wall.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's blinking and later crying suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was deeply disappointed about losing but held back her tears until she had congratulated her opponent.

qa.q: Why was Coach Himani's choice to sit silently a good one?
qa.a: It let Pallavi feel her disappointment with support nearby, without rushing her or turning it into a lesson.

qa.q: How might the girl from Andheri remember the final?
qa.a: She would likely remember Pallavi as a kind, fair opponent who praised her smashes even after losing.

grounding: A coach records a child building skill through repeated practice and losing gracefully.

passage: Wednesday. Chess club tournament today. I have practised knight moves every night for a month, even the boring puzzles Uncle printed for me. I won my first two games! Then I played Afreen. She is ten, one year younger than me, and I thought it would be easy. She trapped my queen in fifteen moves. I felt like knocking all the pieces off the board. My face was so hot. But I remembered what Sir says, 'Shake hands first, feel later.' So I said 'good game' through my teeth. It came out weird. Afreen said 'good game' back and showed me where I went wrong. Actually useful. Still annoyed. Practising queen safety tomorrow. — Zubin

qa.q: How many moves did it take Afreen to trap Zubin's queen?
qa.a: Afreen trapped Zubin's queen in fifteen moves.

qa.q: How can you tell Zubin was angry after losing to Afreen?
qa.a: Zubin's face was hot, Zubin felt like knocking the pieces off the board and said 'good game' through gritted teeth.

qa.q: What did Zubin do right after the loss, even though it was hard?
qa.a: Zubin followed Sir's rule, shook hands and listened to Afreen's tips, then planned to practise what went wrong.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Zubin's 'good game'?
qa.a: She may have noticed it sounded strained but still felt respected, since Zubin listened when she pointed out the mistake. 🙂

grounding: A child writes about practising a skill and managing to lose gracefully despite anger.
